There are three things I do in the first two minutes of every call, and I never skip them, even when I am late. First, the sound. I ask whether everybody can hear me, and I wait for an answer, because there is always one person who is on a train. Second, who is in the room. Not the names on the invitation, the people who actually joined, because those are two different lists and only one of them matters. Third, and this is the one people leave until it is too late, I ask how much time we have. If you ask that at the end, the answer is useless. If you ask it at the beginning, you know what to leave out. One more thing, and I say this to everybody I train. Never open a call by apologising for your English. Nobody in twenty years has ended a call because of an accent, and the apology is the only thing they will remember from your first minute.

People think they are being rude when they talk over each other on a call, and almost always they are not. There is about half a second of delay between the two ends, so when you stop, the other person has already started, because for them you stopped half a second ago. It is physics, not manners. What I tell everybody is to stop the moment it happens, say sorry, please go ahead, and let the other person finish the sentence. Whoever stops first is the one who looks like they are in control of the meeting, which is the opposite of what people expect. And on meetings that run over: they never run over at the end. They run over at the beginning, because nobody said out loud how much time there was, so nobody knew which part to drop. Two sentences at the start save you ten minutes at the end.
